title: Compound statements (blocks)
recap: A compound statement, also called a block, groups zero or more statements between braces so the compiler can treat the group as one statement. A block does not need a semicolon after its closing brace.

Blocks can be nested. An if statement can therefore control several related statements with one block, but excessive nesting makes control flow harder to follow and is often a sign that code should be moved into a function.
objectives: Use a block as the statement controlled by an if condition.
Execute two related statements only when a fixed condition is true.
Distinguish a block's braces from list-initialization braces.
Keep the nesting depth small and readable.
warnings: Without a block, an if statement controls only the next statement.
Do not put a semicolon between an if condition and its controlled block.
Avoid adding nested blocks when a separate function would express the work more clearly.
challenge: Start approvedUnits at 0 and set inspectionPassed to true. Use one if statement with a compound statement containing both the assignment of 12 approved units and the inspection message. Then report the final approved unit count outside the conditional block.
hints: The statement controlled by if (inspectionPassed) should begin with { and end with }.
Place both approvedUnits = 12; and the first std::cout statement inside that block.
Print approvedUnits after the block so the final report is not part of the conditional statement.
